records.title: Loaded language
records.definition: Words with strong positive or negative associations that encourage an emotional evaluation beyond the literal information conveyed.

records.title: Ad hominem
records.definition: Attacking a person’s character or circumstances instead of addressing the substance of their argument.
javascript: A personal insult given as grounds to reject the addressee's argument.

records.title: False dilemma
records.definition: Presenting two options as the only possibilities when other reasonable alternatives exist.
records.gap: Requires evidence of another option in the passage.
javascript: A claim of exactly two options alongside a distinct option explicitly named as available.

records.title: Straw man
records.definition: Recasting an opposing position in a weaker or distorted form that is easier to criticise.

records.title: Appeal to fear
records.definition: Using a threat or frightening possibility to influence judgement or action, particularly when supporting evidence is missing or unclear.
pendingRequired: fear used to support a decision or claim

records.title: Bandwagon appeal
records.definition: Suggesting that a claim or action is correct because many people supposedly accept or do it.
javascript: An explicit popularity claim linked to the same recommendation.

records.title: Selective presentation
records.definition: Highlighting evidence that supports a particular conclusion while leaving out relevant counterevidence or context.

records.title: Quote mining
records.definition: Using a quotation while omitting surrounding material that changes or qualifies its meaning.

records.title: Whataboutism
records.definition: Deflecting criticism by pointing to another alleged wrong rather than addressing the original point.

records.title: Appeal to false authority
records.definition: Using a person’s status or claimed expertise as support where their expertise is not relevant or the authority is not established.
pendingRequired: lack of relevant expertise or established authority

records.title: Conspiracy framing
records.definition: Explaining events through an alleged hidden plan while relying on insinuation or claims that are difficult to test.
pendingRequired: assertion grounded in insinuation or difficult-to-test claims

records.title: Repetition and familiarity
records.definition: Repeating a claim or phrase so that familiarity can make it easier to recall or feel more credible.
records.gap: Covers exact repetition within a paragraph. The reader's response is unknown.
javascript: Verbatim sentence repetition within a paragraph.

records.title: Priming
records.definition: Presenting cues that make particular concepts or associations more accessible when a reader processes later information.
pendingRequired: later material related to the association

records.title: Presupposition
records.definition: Embedding an assumption in a sentence so that it is treated as given rather than argued for.

records.title: False balance
records.definition: Presenting positions as comparably supported when the available evidence is substantially unequal.
records.gap: Relative strength of the available evidence

records.title: Anecdotal evidence
records.definition: Using an individual story as if it establishes a general pattern without adequate supporting data.
records.gap: Covers an explicitly supplied individual story.

records.title: Slippery slope
records.definition: Claiming that one step will lead to a chain of further consequences without adequately establishing the links.

records.title: Scapegoating
records.definition: Assigning broad blame for a complex problem to a person or group while simplifying or ignoring other causes.
pendingRequired: complex problem attributed broadly to a target
available other causes omitted or simplified

records.title: Motte-and-bailey
records.definition: Moving between a bold, controversial claim and a narrower, easier-to-defend claim as criticism arises.
pendingRequired: broad and narrower versions of a claim

records.title: Gish gallop
records.definition: Overwhelming a discussion with numerous claims faster than they can reasonably be checked or answered.

records.title: Allegation laundering
records.definition: An allegation is first reported as a claim, suspicion or accusation. Later references restate it as though the underlying event has been established. The wording changes the status of the information without adding independent evidence.
pendingRequired: later restatement as fact without new evidence
javascript: The same clause first attributed as an allegation and then restated unqualified.

records.title: Insinuation by juxtaposition
records.definition: The article presents separate details in close proximity, allowing their arrangement to suggest a causal, moral or factual connection. The implied conclusion is carried by the juxtaposition rather than demonstrated by evidence.
pendingRequired: implied connection unsupported by the details

records.title: Blame reversal
records.definition: The account makes the complainant's response the main issue, while the original conduct receives less attention or is treated as justified by that response.
pendingRequired: focus shifted to the complainant's response

records.title: Retaliatory discrediting of complainants
records.definition: The article frames a person as unreliable, malicious or troublesome because they made a complaint or report. The fact that a report is disputed or unsubstantiated is treated as evidence that it was knowingly false.
pendingRequired: source credibility attacked because of the act of reporting

records.title: Manufactured consensus
records.definition: The text uses selected reactions, vague references to public opinion or unsupported claims of widespread agreement to create an impression of consensus.

records.title: Appeal to guilt
records.definition: The text connects disagreement, inaction or a particular choice with guilt for harm to others, without adequately establishing the reader's responsibility or the effectiveness of the proposed response.
javascript: An explicit test of care tying a named person's distress to an instruction.

records.title: Obfuscation and strategic vagueness
records.definition: The text obscures the relevant actor, action, evidence or degree of certainty through vague language, nominalisations, passive constructions or undefined terms.
pendingRequired: identifiable missing actor, action, evidence or certainty

records.title: Semantic diversion
records.definition: The text isolates a literal interpretation of a word or phrase, then uses that interpretation to dismiss the wider point. The disputed wording becomes a substitute for engaging with the underlying evidence.
pendingRequired: minor wording dispute used in place of a response

records.title: Moving the goalposts
records.definition: The article or argument introduces a criterion, receives evidence meeting it, and then replaces it with a more demanding or different criterion without explaining why the change is justified.
javascript: An explicitly sufficient criterion repeated as fulfilled before an additional requirement is introduced.

records.title: Double standards
records.definition: The text treats similar actions differently depending on who performs them, or demands evidence from one side while accepting weaker support from another.

records.title: Poisoning the well
records.definition: The text introduces a source using a negative label or allegation that encourages readers to reject what the source says, without evaluating the substance of the evidence.
pendingRequired: later claims discounted on that basis

records.title: Criminalising dissent
records.definition: The text uses criminal labels or law-and-order language to associate a viewpoint or group with illegality, sometimes blurring the distinction between lawful dissent, alleged offences and proven criminal conduct.
pendingRequired: criminal label unsupported by the conduct described

records.title: Appearance-based personal attack
records.definition: The text directs ridicule or contempt at appearance rather than engaging with the person's claims or conduct relevant to the issue.
pendingRequired: ridicule replaces engagement with relevant conduct or claims
records.gap: Covers explicit appearance insults tied to dismissal of the same person's position.
javascript: An appearance insult explicitly used to dismiss the same person's stated position.

records.title: Appeal to disgust
records.definition: The text relies on descriptions associated with dirt, contamination, bodily functions or repulsiveness to influence judgement beyond what the factual account establishes.
pendingRequired: description used to influence a judgement

records.title: Threat framing
records.definition: The text uses warnings, predictions of punishment or threatening language to make a particular response seem necessary. The consequence may be real, exaggerated, speculative or unsupported.
javascript: An explicit adverse consequence imposed by the speaker for refusing to act.

records.title: Premature closure
records.definition: The text uses definitive language to close down further examination, despite unresolved evidence, unanswered questions or acknowledged uncertainty.
pendingRequired: acknowledged or otherwise visible unresolved evidence

records.title: Narrative reframing
records.definition: The article selects a starting point, sequence, protagonists and causal links that create a particular account of events. The individual details may be accurate while the overall narrative gives them a selective meaning.
pendingRequired: selected sequence, roles or causal links
comparison context for the inferred shift

records.title: Quote recontextualisation
records.definition: The article selects a phrase, sentence or excerpt but omits surrounding context, qualifications or the question it answered. This can make a limited or conditional statement appear broader or more definite.

records.title: Public shaming
records.definition: The text invites readers to condemn or mock an identifiable person, often by foregrounding humiliating details or presenting social rejection as deserved.
pendingRequired: invitation to ridicule or condemn in public

records.title: Paternalistic coercion framing
records.definition: The text uses protective language to frame a restriction, punishment or demand as care, while giving little attention to consent, proportionality, alternatives or the interests of those affected.
pendingRequired: justification as care for the affected person

records.title: Incitement to violence
records.definition: The text urges, endorses or legitimises violent action against an identifiable person, group or category of people. It may use direct commands, calls for action, celebration of violence or language that presents violence as necessary or deserved.
pendingRequired: target identifiable by person, group or category

records.title: Exaggeration and minimisation
records.definition: The text amplifies or downplays the scale, severity, certainty or importance of something. This may happen through evaluative wording, selective comparisons, numerical presentation or omission of relevant context.
pendingRequired: comparison evidence supporting a material discrepancy

records.title: Firsthand evidence requirement
records.definition: The argument dismisses or refuses to engage with evidence because the person presenting it did not personally witness the event. It treats direct observation as the only legitimate route to knowledge, rather than assessing what the available photographs, documents, recordings or other evidence can support. Firsthand observation may provide additional evidence, but its absence does not by itself invalidate other evidence.
javascript: Other evidence explicitly rejected because the addressee did not witness the event.

records.title: Invoking an imagined audience
records.definition: The speaker predicts or asserts how an absent person, institution or audience will react, and uses that imagined reaction to influence the listener. The audience may be a specific group, such as the press, a jury, the police or an employer, or a vague collective such as 'everyone'. Rather than addressing the issue directly, the statement imports the supposed judgement of others into the conversation. The prediction can make the listener feel watched, outnumbered, judged or threatened, even though the people whose reactions are invoked have not expressed those views.
pendingRequired: absent audience's reaction asserted or predicted
reaction used as pressure or implied opposition

records.title: Hasty generalisation
records.definition: A conclusion about a whole group or general pattern is drawn from a small, unrepresentative or otherwise inadequate sample. The examples may be real, but they do not justify the breadth of the conclusion.
javascript: One or two observations explicitly generalized to all members of the same named group.

records.title: Circular reasoning
records.definition: The argument assumes the point it is supposed to prove. Its supporting reason simply repeats the conclusion in different words rather than providing independent evidence.
javascript: An exact restatement or an allowlisted synonymous restatement used as the reason.

records.title: Appeal to authority
records.definition: A claim is presented as established because a prominent or authoritative person endorses it. The person's status is substituted for relevant expertise, evidence or reasoning.
records.gap: Evidence of an appeal alone cannot establish whether reliance on the authority is justified.
javascript: A credential explicitly treated as sufficient reason to accept a claim.

records.title: Post hoc (false cause)
records.definition: The argument treats a sequence in time as proof of causation. The fact that one event preceded another does not establish that it caused it.
javascript: The order of two explicitly matched events offered as the entire basis for causation.

records.title: Red herring
records.definition: The argument shifts attention away from the original question by introducing a separate issue that does not answer it.
pendingRequired: irrelevant issue used to divert attention

records.title: Appeal to emotion
records.definition: The argument asks the audience to accept a conclusion because of the feelings it evokes, rather than because of evidence or reasoning that supports it.
pendingRequired: emotion offered as a reason to accept a claim

records.title: Tu quoque (hypocrisy)
records.definition: Instead of addressing whether the criticism is valid, the response points to the critic's own behaviour or inconsistency. A person's hypocrisy does not by itself make their argument false.
javascript: The addressee's alleged inconsistency explicitly used to dismiss a criticism.

records.title: Appeal to ignorance
records.definition: The absence of proof for one side is treated as proof for the other. A lack of disproof does not establish that a claim is true.
javascript: A lack of disproof explicitly declared sufficient proof.

records.title: False equivalence
records.definition: The argument presents two things as equivalent while overlooking differences that matter to the comparison. The comparison creates a misleading impression of similarity.
pendingRequired: material difference relevant to the comparison

records.title: Cherry picking
records.definition: The argument highlights favourable examples or data while excluding relevant contrary evidence, creating a misleading impression of what the full evidence shows.

records.title: Preference as moral obligation
records.definition: A speaker moves from 'I prefer this' to 'you must do this', then portrays disagreement or noncompliance as proof of disrespect or bad character. The personal preference is used as its own justification for a moral duty, without addressing context, proportionality or any independent reason for the demand.
pendingRequired: unsupported obligation and condemnation of noncompliance

records.title: Too good to be true
records.definition: An offer presents an exceptional financial gain, prize, inheritance or other benefit as readily available, then asks the recipient to pay a relatively small fee, follow a link, share sensitive information or take another apparently minor step to obtain it. The disproportionate reward can draw attention away from whether the offer is genuine. The pattern concerns the structure of the offer, not the literal phrase 'too good to be true'.
javascript: An immediate guaranteed cash return of at least 100 times the requested payment in the same currency.

records.title: Deliberate errors
records.definition: Introducing a conspicuous spelling mistake or other apparent error can interrupt ordinary reading and draw extra attention to the affected word or sentence. A particularly important mechanism is correction bait: the reader feels prompted to point out the mistake, creating engagement with a message they might otherwise ignore. The exchange can divert attention from the original argument and, on some social platforms, may help distribute the post further. Mistakes can also make a prepared message appear spontaneous. These are possible effects, not proof that the error was intentional. A further possible effect follows when a correction becomes a personal insult: readers who identify with the speaker's position may experience the insult as directed at people like themselves. This can shift the discussion from the claim's merits to defending the speaker or group.
records.gap: Intent cannot be established from a spelling observation

records.title: Moral authority as a substitute for argument
records.definition: The speaker appeals to an important moral value, such as dignity, fairness or protecting others, and treats that value as sufficient reason to end a disagreement. Rather than explaining what is wrong with a particular claim, the speaker labels the act of questioning it as immoral. The principle may be entirely reasonable; the manipulation lies in using its moral authority as a substitute for reasoning. The result can be outward compliance without any change in belief.
pendingRequired: principle used to delegitimise questioning rather than address a claim

records.title: Provoking backlash
records.definition: A broadly defensible principle is presented together with a rigid, humiliating or disproportionate demand. People who might otherwise agree with the principle can come to associate it with coercion and react against it. The pressure can shift attention away from the reason for the principle and towards resistance to how it is enforced. This can be exploited by someone seeking to discredit the principle, but neither hostile intent nor a deliberate plan can be inferred from the wording alone.
pendingRequired: defensible principle coupled to disproportionate pressure
actual reaction or intent requires other evidence

records.title: Turning disagreement into a freedom conflict
records.definition: A question about the accuracy, fairness or merits of a statement is reframed as a question about the speaker's freedom to express it. Criticism, disagreement, social pressure and actual restrictions on speech can be blurred together. If the audience feels its freedom is threatened, defending the right to speak may displace examination of the original claim. The freedom issue may sometimes be genuine; identifying this pattern means checking whether it has replaced, rather than answered, the original argument.
javascript: A direct objection to the claim recast as a denial of permission to speak.

records.title: Manufactured inevitability
records.definition: A decision, rule or outcome is presented as though it cannot be changed, challenged or interpreted differently simply because it has already been named or declared. Repeating a term in an identity statement (X is X, or X means X) adds no premise that establishes necessity, yet can rhetorically suggest that alternatives are impossible or questioning is illegitimate. The pattern concerns the gap between this logically empty assertion and the stronger conclusion the reader is invited to accept. Genuine legal, technical or practical constraints are separate evidence and must be assessed on their merits.
pendingRequired: repeated naming or existence offered as its own justification
records.gap: Covers explicit claims of necessity based on an identical label or mere existence.
javascript: An identical label offered as the stated reason an outcome cannot change.

records.title: Attack conflation
records.definition: Attack conflation is a shift in what a criticism is taken to target. A remark about presentation (such as a spelling mistake) is used or understood as a judgement on the argument, then on the speaker's intelligence or character, and sometimes on anyone who shares the speaker's view. The shift can come from a critic treating an error as proof that the claim or its author is worthless, or from a respondent interpreting a narrow correction as a broader personal or group attack. The broader conclusion must be distinguished from what was actually criticised. This is a descriptive label for an observable change in meaning, not an established psychological diagnosis or evidence of deliberate intent.
javascript: A correction of one item explicitly recast as an attack on a wider group or argument.

records.title: Restoring agency
records.definition: The wording explicitly leaves the decision with the person affected.
javascript: Explicit permission to decide paired with explicit acceptance of either choice.

records.title: Welcoming disagreement
records.definition: The speaker invites objections and engages with their substance without ridicule or penalty.
javascript: An explicit invitation to identify an error or disagree.

records.title: Separating observation from interpretation
records.definition: The account labels observations, inferences and unanswered questions separately.
javascript: An explicitly identified observation followed by an expressly uncertain interpretation.

records.title: Acknowledging uncertainty
records.definition: The speaker identifies what they do not know and calibrates confidence to the available information.
javascript: The speaker explicitly qualifies their own first-person claim.

records.title: Respecting boundaries
records.definition: After a boundary is stated, the speaker changes course or ends that line of discussion.
records.gap: Covers explicit acceptance of a stated boundary.
javascript: A request for space or no calls followed by a directly related commitment.

records.title: Proportionate response
records.definition: The language avoids inflating a minor problem and proposes a response appropriate to its likely impact.

records.title: Encouraging independent thought
records.definition: The speaker offers reasons or information while explicitly allowing independent assessment.
javascript: An explicit invitation to check figures, evidence or sources independently.

records.title: Validating emotional experience
records.definition: The response acknowledges the feeling and its impact without asserting an unverified explanation.
javascript: Explicit acknowledgement that the other person's feeling makes sense.

records.title: Transparent reasoning
records.definition: The speaker explains the evidence, assumptions and steps leading to their conclusion.
records.gap: Covers a reason that supports a stated conclusion.
javascript: A conclusion restating the explicitly universal property of an explicitly named member.

records.title: Supporting informed choice
records.definition: The communication presents meaningful alternatives and material trade-offs without hiding inconvenient information.

records.title: Taking responsibility
records.definition: The speaker identifies what they did, recognises the impact and states a practical corrective step.
javascript: An admission of a specific mistake followed by acceptance of responsibility.

records.title: Respecting attention
records.definition: The speaker makes the request clear, gives a reasonable timeframe and accepts that the person may respond later or decline.
records.gap: Covers an explicit option to disengage.
javascript: Explicit permission to skip the rest or stop reading.

records.title: Conclusion supported by the premises
records.definition: The reasoning is consistent when its conclusion follows from the premises, or when the available evidence reasonably supports a qualified conclusion. This is a positive assessment of the argument's structure, not a guarantee that the premises are true or that no relevant evidence is missing.
javascript: A conclusion restating the explicitly universal property of an explicitly named member.

records.title: Freedom of choice followed by pressure
records.definition: Language that offers free choice is immediately undercut by a demand, penalty or threat tied to that choice.
records.gap: Covers a penalty tied to declining the stated choice.
javascript: Explicit permission to refuse followed by a penalty explicitly tied to refusal.

records.title: Respect for disagreement followed by punishment
records.definition: An invitation to disagree is immediately reversed by a rule or consequence punishing disagreement.
pendingRequired: penalty tied to the same person's disagreement
javascript: Permission to disagree directly followed by a sanction for the same disagreement.

records.title: Empathy followed by guilt or conditional approval
records.definition: Acknowledging someone's feelings is immediately followed by guilt or a demand presented as a test of loyalty or care.
pendingRequired: connected demand framed as loyalty or care
javascript: Acknowledgement of an expressed feeling followed by a demand framed as a test of loyalty.

records.title: Independent thinking followed by enforced agreement
records.definition: An invitation to make up your own mind is followed by a demand that the reader accept the speaker's view.
pendingRequired: same person's decision restricted to the speaker's view
javascript: An invitation to decide independently directly reversed by a demand to agree.
